name: Brain
description: Cerebral cortex (gyri of both hemispheres), deep structures, ventricles, brainstem and cerebellum.

source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Brain
groups.tip: Brain divisions: forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus), midbrain, and hindbrain (pons, medulla, cerebellum). Some cortex, including the frontal pole and inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area), is not included in this model.

groups.label: Left cerebral hemisphere (gyri)
groups.tip: Central sulcus rule: precentral = motor ("pre = go"), postcentral = sensory. In most people the left hemisphere is dominant for language, including the Wernicke area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus.

groups.label: Right cerebral hemisphere (gyri)
groups.tip: Each hemisphere controls and feels the opposite side of the body. The right hemisphere is usually more involved in spatial attention, face recognition and the emotional tone of speech.

groups.label: Deep structures
groups.tip: Basal ganglia: caudate + putamen = striatum; putamen + globus pallidus = lentiform ("lens-shaped") nucleus. The limbic trio: hippocampus (memory), amygdala (fear), fornix (the arch linking them to the hypothalamus).

groups.label: Ventricles
groups.tip: CSF route: lateral ventricles -> interventricular foramina -> third ventricle -> cerebral aqueduct -> fourth ventricle -> apertures (Magendie median, Luschka lateral) -> subarachnoid space.

groups.label: Brainstem and cerebellum
groups.tip: Cranial nerve "rule of 4s": nerves III-IV from the midbrain, V-VIII from the pons, IX-XII from the medulla (I and II attach to the forebrain).

content.origin: Latin frons, "forehead", and Greek gyros, "circle" or "ring" (a gyrus is a raised fold of cortex).
content.location: The uppermost fold of the left frontal lobe, running from front to back beside the midline and continuing onto the medial surface of the hemisphere.
content.description: A long strip of cortex bordered below by the superior frontal sulcus and behind by the precentral gyrus. The frontal pole and inferior frontal gyrus are not included in this model.
content.function: Its back part on the medial surface contains the supplementary motor area, which helps plan and sequence movements. The rest is prefrontal cortex involved in self-awareness, working memory and control of behaviour.
content.mnemonic: Frontal lobe = "front office": the superior gyrus is the top floor where plans are made.
content.clinical: Damage to the frontal lobes, including this gyrus, can change personality, motivation and judgement. An anterior cerebral artery stroke affects its medial surface.
content.hint: The top fold at the front of the hemisphere, lying alongside the longitudinal fissure.

questions.text: Which gyrus forms the uppermost fold of the frontal lobe beside the midline?
questions.explanation: The superior frontal gyrus runs along the top of the frontal lobe next to the longitudinal fissure.

content.origin: Latin medius, "middle", and frons, "forehead".
content.location: On the lateral surface of the left frontal lobe, between the superior and inferior frontal sulci and in front of the precentral gyrus.
content.description: A broad horizontal fold, often partly divided by a shallow groove. The inferior frontal gyrus below it is not included in this model.
content.function: Its back part contains the frontal eye field, which moves both eyes voluntarily towards the opposite side. Its front part is dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, used for working memory, planning and attention.
content.mnemonic: Middle frontal = "mind's eye": it steers the eyes and holds plans in mind.
content.clinical: After an acute stroke that damages the frontal eye field, the eyes tend to look towards the side of the damaged hemisphere.
content.hint: The horizontal fold in the middle of the lateral frontal lobe, sandwiched between the top frontal fold and the missing lowest one.

questions.text: Which area in the back of the middle frontal gyrus controls voluntary eye movements?
questions.explanation: The frontal eye field in the posterior middle frontal gyrus directs voluntary gaze.

content.origin: Latin prae, "in front of", and centralis: the gyrus in front of the central sulcus.
content.location: The last fold of the left frontal lobe, lying directly in front of the central sulcus and running from the top of the hemisphere down towards the lateral sulcus.
content.description: A long vertical strip of cortex. Its motor map (the motor homunculus) has the leg near the midline, then the trunk, arm and hand, with the face lowest.
content.function: Primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4). It sends commands down the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts to control voluntary movement of the opposite side of the body. The left gyrus serves the right side of the body.
content.mnemonic: "Pre = go": the precentral gyrus makes you move; the postcentral gyrus lets you feel.
content.clinical: A stroke here causes weakness of the opposite side of the body. Middle cerebral artery strokes mostly affect the face and arm, anterior cerebral artery strokes the leg.
content.hint: The vertical strip just in front of the central sulcus; it holds the body map for voluntary movement.

questions.text: The precentral gyrus contains which functional area?
questions.explanation: The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex (area 4).

questions.text: A stroke in the left precentral gyrus would most likely cause what?
options: Weakness of the left side of the body
Loss of vision in both eyes
Weakness of the right side of the body
questions.explanation: Each motor cortex controls the opposite side of the body because the motor pathway crosses in the medulla.

content.origin: Latin post, "behind", and centralis: the gyrus behind the central sulcus.
content.location: The first fold of the left parietal lobe, lying directly behind the central sulcus and parallel to the precentral gyrus.
content.description: A long vertical strip of cortex with a sensory body map (the sensory homunculus): leg near the midline and face lowest, with large areas for the hands and lips.
content.function: Primary somatosensory cortex (Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2). It receives touch, pressure, pain, temperature and body-position information from the opposite side of the body, relayed through the thalamus. The left gyrus serves the right side of the body.
content.mnemonic: "Post = post office": the postcentral gyrus receives the incoming sensory mail.
content.clinical: Damage causes loss of fine touch and position sense on the opposite side of the body, making it hard to recognise objects by feel.
content.hint: The vertical strip just behind the central sulcus, first stop in the cortex for touch.

questions.text: The postcentral gyrus lies in which lobe?
questions.explanation: It is the most anterior gyrus of the parietal lobe, just behind the central sulcus.

questions.text: Which sensation is processed mainly in the postcentral gyrus?
questions.explanation: The postcentral gyrus is the primary somatosensory cortex for touch, pain, temperature and position sense.

content.origin: Latin paries, "wall" (the parietal bones form the side walls of the skull); lobulus, "small lobe"; precuneus, "in front of the wedge" (the cuneus).
content.location: The upper part of the left parietal lobe behind the postcentral gyrus, above the intraparietal sulcus, continuing onto the medial surface as the precuneus.
content.description: A block of cortex on the upper lateral surface of the parietal lobe. In this model it is combined with the precuneus, the part of the parietal lobe on the medial surface.
content.function: Somatosensory and visual association cortex. It combines touch, body position and vision to build a sense of where the body and nearby objects are in space, guiding reaching and grasping.
content.mnemonic: Superior parietal = "sat-nav" of the body: it tells you where your limbs are.
content.clinical: Damage can cause difficulty reaching accurately for objects under visual guidance (optic ataxia) and problems sensing limb position on the opposite side.
content.hint: The upper back part of the parietal lobe, above the intraparietal sulcus, wrapping onto the medial surface.

questions.text: What is the main role of the superior parietal lobule?
options: Combining touch and vision to sense body position in space
questions.explanation: It is association cortex that integrates somatosensory and visual information for spatial awareness and reaching.

content.origin: Latin supra, "above", and margo, "edge": it arches over the end of the lateral sulcus.
content.location: In the left inferior parietal lobule, curving around the posterior end of the lateral sulcus, behind the lower postcentral gyrus.
content.description: A horseshoe-shaped gyrus capping the back end of the lateral sulcus. It is the front part of the inferior parietal lobule; the angular gyrus lies behind it.
content.function: Association cortex for touch and body position, and for planning skilled learned movements. In the left (usually language-dominant) hemisphere it also helps process the sounds of words (phonological processing).
content.mnemonic: "Supra-marginal sits on the margin": it sits on the end of the lateral sulcus like a cap.
content.clinical: Damage to the left inferior parietal lobule, including this gyrus, can cause ideomotor apraxia: difficulty performing learned gestures on command despite normal strength.
content.hint: The horseshoe fold capping the posterior end of the lateral sulcus, just behind the lower postcentral gyrus.

questions.text: The supramarginal gyrus curves around the end of which sulcus?
questions.explanation: The supramarginal gyrus caps the posterior end of the lateral (Sylvian) sulcus.

content.origin: Latin angulus, "angle" or "bend": it bends around the end of the superior temporal sulcus.
content.location: In the back of the left inferior parietal lobule, behind the supramarginal gyrus, curving around the end of the superior temporal sulcus near the occipital lobe.
content.description: A curved gyrus at the meeting point of the parietal, temporal and occipital lobes.
content.function: A multimodal association area linking vision, hearing and touch. In the left (usually dominant) hemisphere it is important for reading, writing, calculation and the meaning of words.
content.mnemonic: Angular gyrus = "reading corner": the angle where seeing words meets understanding them.
content.clinical: Damage to the left angular gyrus can cause Gerstmann syndrome: difficulty writing and calculating, confusing left and right, and failing to name fingers. It can also cause loss of reading and writing.
content.hint: The curved fold where parietal, temporal and occipital lobes meet, behind the horseshoe that caps the lateral sulcus.

questions.text: A lesion of the left angular gyrus is most likely to affect which ability?
questions.explanation: In the dominant hemisphere the angular gyrus is important for reading, writing and calculation.

content.origin: Latin tempus, "time" (the temples, where hair first greys with age).
content.location: The top fold of the left temporal lobe, just below the lateral sulcus. Its upper surface, hidden inside the sulcus, carries the transverse temporal gyri.
content.description: A long horizontal gyrus. In this model it includes the transverse temporal (Heschl) gyri, the small folds on its upper surface that hold the primary auditory cortex.
content.function: Contains the primary auditory cortex (Brodmann areas 41 and 42) on the transverse temporal gyri, which receives hearing information from both ears, plus surrounding auditory association cortex. In most people the back part of the left superior temporal gyrus is the Wernicke area, which is essential for understanding spoken language.
content.mnemonic: "Superior temporal = superior hearing": the ears sit next to the temporal lobes.
content.clinical: Damage to the Wernicke area (usually left) causes Wernicke (receptive) aphasia: fluent speech that makes little sense and poor understanding of what others say.
content.hint: The top fold of the lobe that lies beside the ear, just below the lateral sulcus; its hidden upper surface receives sound.

questions.text: The transverse temporal gyri on the superior temporal gyrus contain which area?
questions.explanation: The primary auditory cortex (areas 41 and 42) lies on the transverse temporal (Heschl) gyri.

questions.text: Damage to the posterior left superior temporal gyrus most typically causes which problem?
questions.explanation: This region is the Wernicke area; damage causes receptive (Wernicke) aphasia.

content.origin: Latin medius, "middle", and tempus, "temple".
content.location: On the lateral surface of the left temporal lobe, between the superior and inferior temporal gyri.
content.description: A long horizontal fold between the superior and inferior temporal sulci, reaching back towards the occipital lobe.
content.function: Association cortex involved in understanding the meaning of words and in memory for facts. Its back end, near the occipital lobe, helps detect visual motion. On the left it supports word meaning (semantics) as part of the language network.
content.mnemonic: Middle temporal = "middle man": it links sounds and sights to their meaning.
content.clinical: It is a common site for temporal lobe epilepsy spread and for tumours; damage on the left can cause word-finding difficulty.
content.hint: The middle of the three horizontal folds on the side of the lobe below the lateral sulcus.

questions.text: Which gyrus lies between the superior and inferior temporal gyri?
questions.explanation: The middle temporal gyrus lies between the superior and inferior temporal sulci.

content.origin: Latin inferior, "lower", and tempus, "temple".
content.location: The lowest fold of the lateral surface of the left temporal lobe, curving onto its underside next to the fusiform gyrus.
content.description: A horizontal gyrus below the inferior temporal sulcus, forming the lower lateral edge of the temporal lobe.
content.function: Higher visual cortex in the ventral "what" pathway. It helps recognise objects, shapes and colours.
content.mnemonic: Inferior temporal = "identify things": it answers "what am I looking at?".
content.clinical: Damage to the ventral visual pathway, including this region, can cause visual agnosia: seeing an object but being unable to recognise it.
content.hint: The lowest fold on the side of the lobe beside the ear, wrapping onto the underside of the brain.

questions.text: The inferior temporal gyrus is part of which visual pathway?
options: The pathway to the superior colliculus for reflexes
questions.explanation: The inferior temporal gyrus lies in the ventral stream, which recognises what objects are.

content.origin: Latin occiput, "back of the head" (ob, "against", and caput, "head").
content.location: The rear lobe of the left cerebral hemisphere, behind the parietal and temporal lobes and resting on the tentorium cerebelli above the cerebellum.
content.description: A pyramid-shaped lobe. Its medial surface is divided by the calcarine sulcus into the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below.
content.function: The visual lobe. Primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) lines the calcarine sulcus and receives input from the opposite half of the visual field of both eyes; the surrounding cortex is visual association cortex.
content.mnemonic: "O for optic": the occipital lobe is for seeing, at the back of the head.
content.clinical: A posterior cerebral artery stroke in one occipital lobe causes loss of the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes (homonymous hemianopia), often with sparing of central vision.
content.hint: The rearmost lobe of the hemisphere, sitting above the cerebellum; the calcarine sulcus runs through it.

questions.text: Primary visual cortex lies along which sulcus in the occipital lobe?
questions.explanation: Primary visual cortex (area 17) lines the calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital lobe.

questions.text: A stroke in the left occipital lobe would cause loss of which part of vision?
options: The right half of the visual field in both eyes
The left half of the visual field in both eyes
All vision in the left eye only
questions.explanation: Each occipital lobe receives the opposite visual field, so a left lesion causes a right homonymous hemianopia.

content.origin: Latin insula, "island": it is an island of cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus.
content.location: Deep inside the left lateral sulcus, hidden beneath the overlying frontal, parietal and temporal lobes (the opercula), lateral to the lentiform nucleus.
content.description: A triangular area of cortex with short and long gyri, surrounded by the circular sulcus. It can only be seen when the lips of the lateral sulcus are pulled apart.
content.function: Primary taste (gustatory) cortex, and processing of internal body sensations such as heartbeat, breathing, pain and gut feelings, linking them with emotion.
content.mnemonic: "Insula = inside": the hidden island that feels your insides.
content.clinical: Strokes of the middle cerebral artery often damage the insula because its branches run over it.
content.hint: Cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the lips of three lobes; taste is processed here.

questions.text: Where is the insula found?
options: On the medial surface of the occipital lobe
On the top of the frontal lobe
questions.explanation: The insula is hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the opercula.

questions.text: Which primary sensory area is located in the insula?
questions.explanation: The insula contains the primary gustatory cortex.

content.origin: Latin cingulum, "belt" or "girdle": it wraps around the corpus callosum like a belt.
content.location: On the medial surface of the left hemisphere, arching around the top of the corpus callosum from front to back.
content.description: A C-shaped gyrus between the callosal sulcus below and the cingulate sulcus above. Behind the splenium of the corpus callosum it narrows (the isthmus) and continues into the parahippocampal gyrus.
content.function: Part of the limbic system. The front part helps with emotion, motivation, the unpleasantness of pain and attention; the back part helps with memory and self-reflection.
content.mnemonic: Cingulate = "cingulum" belt: it belts around the corpus callosum.
content.clinical: Swelling in one hemisphere can push the cingulate gyrus under the falx cerebri (subfalcine herniation), compressing the anterior cerebral arteries.
content.hint: A belt of cortex on the medial surface, curving directly over the large white-matter bridge between hemispheres.

questions.text: The cingulate gyrus arches directly above which structure?
questions.explanation: The cingulate gyrus wraps around the upper surface of the corpus callosum.

questions.text: The name cingulate comes from the Latin for what?
questions.explanation: Cingulum means belt or girdle; the gyrus belts around the corpus callosum.

content.origin: Greek para, "beside", and hippocampus, "seahorse": the gyrus beside the hippocampus.
content.location: On the inferior and medial surface of the left temporal lobe, alongside the hippocampus, with the fusiform gyrus lateral to it.
content.description: A gyrus whose front end hooks back on itself to form the uncus. Its front part contains the entorhinal cortex, the main gateway into the hippocampus.
content.function: Part of the limbic system. It passes information from the cortex to the hippocampus for forming new memories, and helps recognise places and scenes.
content.mnemonic: Para-hippocampal = "partner of the hippocampus": it feeds memories in.
content.clinical: Raised pressure above the tentorium can push the uncus over the tentorial edge (uncal herniation), compressing the oculomotor nerve and causing a dilated pupil on that side.
content.hint: The inner fold on the underside of the lobe beside the ear, lying next to the seahorse-shaped memory structure and ending in a hook (the uncus).

questions.text: The parahippocampal gyrus passes information into which structure for memory formation?
questions.explanation: The entorhinal cortex of the parahippocampal gyrus is the main input to the hippocampus.

content.origin: Latin fusus, "spindle", and forma, "shape": it is spindle-shaped, wide in the middle and tapering at each end.
content.location: On the underside of the left temporal and occipital lobes, between the inferior temporal gyrus laterally and the parahippocampal gyrus medially.
content.description: A long spindle-shaped gyrus on the basal surface of the brain, separated from the parahippocampal gyrus by the collateral sulcus.
content.function: High-level visual cortex. It contains areas specialised for recognising faces and, on the left, written words. On the left it includes the visual word form area used in reading.
content.mnemonic: "Fusiform for faces": both start with F.
content.clinical: Damage to the fusiform face area (especially on the right or both sides) can cause prosopagnosia, an inability to recognise familiar faces.
content.hint: A spindle-shaped fold on the underside of the brain, between the lowest lateral temporal fold and the gyrus next to the hippocampus; it recognises faces.

questions.text: Damage to the fusiform gyrus may cause which condition?
questions.explanation: The fusiform face area is specialised for recognising faces.

content.origin: Latin cingulum, "belt" or "girdle": it wraps around the corpus callosum like a belt.
content.location: On the medial surface of the right hemisphere, arching around the top of the corpus callosum from front to back.
content.description: A C-shaped gyrus between the callosal sulcus below and the cingulate sulcus above. Behind the splenium of the corpus callosum it narrows (the isthmus) and continues into the parahippocampal gyrus.
content.function: Part of the limbic system. The front part helps with emotion, motivation, the unpleasantness of pain and attention; the back part helps with memory and self-reflection.
content.mnemonic: Cingulate = "cingulum" belt: it belts around the corpus callosum.
content.clinical: Swelling in one hemisphere can push the cingulate gyrus under the falx cerebri (subfalcine herniation), compressing the anterior cerebral arteries.
content.hint: A belt of cortex on the medial surface, curving directly over the large white-matter bridge between hemispheres.

content.origin: Greek para, "beside", and hippocampus, "seahorse": the gyrus beside the hippocampus.
content.location: On the inferior and medial surface of the right temporal lobe, alongside the hippocampus, with the fusiform gyrus lateral to it.
content.description: A gyrus whose front end hooks back on itself to form the uncus. Its front part contains the entorhinal cortex, the main gateway into the hippocampus.
content.function: Part of the limbic system. It passes information from the cortex to the hippocampus for forming new memories, and helps recognise places and scenes.
content.mnemonic: Para-hippocampal = "partner of the hippocampus": it feeds memories in.
content.clinical: Raised pressure above the tentorium can push the uncus over the tentorial edge (uncal herniation), compressing the oculomotor nerve and causing a dilated pupil on that side.
content.hint: The inner fold on the underside of the lobe beside the ear, lying next to the seahorse-shaped memory structure and ending in a hook (the uncus).

content.origin: Latin fusus, "spindle", and forma, "shape": it is spindle-shaped, wide in the middle and tapering at each end.
content.location: On the underside of the right temporal and occipital lobes, between the inferior temporal gyrus laterally and the parahippocampal gyrus medially.
content.description: A long spindle-shaped gyrus on the basal surface of the brain, separated from the parahippocampal gyrus by the collateral sulcus.
content.function: High-level visual cortex. It contains areas specialised for recognising faces and, on the left, written words. Face recognition is usually stronger in the right fusiform gyrus.
content.mnemonic: "Fusiform for faces": both start with F.
content.clinical: Damage to the fusiform face area (especially on the right or both sides) can cause prosopagnosia, an inability to recognise familiar faces.
content.hint: A spindle-shaped fold on the underside of the brain, between the lowest lateral temporal fold and the gyrus next to the hippocampus; it recognises faces.

content.origin: Latin corpus, "body", and callosus, "tough" or "hard".
content.location: In the midline at the bottom of the longitudinal fissure, joining the two cerebral hemispheres and forming the roof of the lateral ventricles.
content.description: A thick, curved band of white matter with four parts from front to back: rostrum, genu, body and splenium. It is the largest commissure of the brain.
content.function: Carries hundreds of millions of nerve fibres between matching areas of the left and right hemispheres, so the two sides can share information and work together.
content.mnemonic: "Callosum connects": the corpus callosum is the bridge between the two halves.
content.clinical: Cutting the corpus callosum (callosotomy) is sometimes used to stop severe seizures spreading between hemispheres; afterwards the hemispheres cannot easily share information ("split brain").
content.hint: The large arched white-matter bridge seen in the midline between the two hemispheres, with the cingulate cortex curving above it.

questions.text: What is the main role of the corpus callosum?
options: Connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres
questions.explanation: It is the largest commissure, carrying fibres between the two hemispheres.

questions.text: Which part of the corpus callosum is at its posterior end?
questions.explanation: The splenium is the thick posterior end of the corpus callosum.

content.origin: Greek thalamos, "inner chamber" or "bedroom".
content.location: Deep in the left half of the forebrain (diencephalon), forming the side wall of the third ventricle, above the hypothalamus and medial to the basal ganglia.
content.description: An egg-shaped mass of grey matter made of many nuclei. The two thalami are often joined across the third ventricle by a small bridge (the interthalamic adhesion).
content.function: The main relay station to the cerebral cortex: almost all sensory information (except smell) passes through it, and it relays motor loops from the basal ganglia and cerebellum. It also helps regulate alertness and consciousness.
content.mnemonic: "Thalamus = the brain's switchboard": every sense except smell is switched through it.
content.clinical: A thalamic stroke can cause loss of sensation on the opposite side of the body and sometimes severe, burning pain afterwards (thalamic pain syndrome).
content.hint: An egg-shaped grey-matter mass in the centre of the brain, forming the side wall of the slit-like midline ventricle; the relay for incoming senses.

questions.text: Which sense does NOT relay through the thalamus before reaching the cortex?
questions.explanation: Smell (olfaction) is the one sense that reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay.

questions.text: The thalamus forms the side wall of which ventricle?
questions.explanation: The two thalami form the lateral walls of the third ventricle.

content.origin: Greek thalamos, "inner chamber" or "bedroom".
content.location: Deep in the right half of the forebrain (diencephalon), forming the side wall of the third ventricle, above the hypothalamus and medial to the basal ganglia.
content.description: An egg-shaped mass of grey matter made of many nuclei. The two thalami are often joined across the third ventricle by a small bridge (the interthalamic adhesion).
content.function: The main relay station to the cerebral cortex: almost all sensory information (except smell) passes through it, and it relays motor loops from the basal ganglia and cerebellum. It also helps regulate alertness and consciousness.
content.mnemonic: "Thalamus = the brain's switchboard": every sense except smell is switched through it.
content.clinical: A thalamic stroke can cause loss of sensation on the opposite side of the body and sometimes severe, burning pain afterwards (thalamic pain syndrome).
content.hint: An egg-shaped grey-matter mass in the centre of the brain, forming the side wall of the slit-like midline ventricle; the relay for incoming senses.

content.origin: Greek hypo, "below", and thalamos, "inner chamber": the part below the thalamus.
content.location: Below the thalamus in the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle, just above the pituitary gland and behind the optic chiasm.
content.description: A small cluster of nuclei, about the size of an almond. The pituitary stalk (infundibulum) hangs from its underside, and the mammillary bodies bulge from its back.
content.function: Controls homeostasis: body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep-wake rhythm, the autonomic nervous system and the pituitary gland. It makes antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin, which are released from the posterior pituitary.
content.mnemonic: The hypothalamus controls the "4 Fs": feeding, fighting, fleeing and reproduction.
content.clinical: Damage to the hypothalamus or pituitary stalk can stop ADH release, causing central diabetes insipidus with large volumes of dilute urine and constant thirst.
content.hint: A small region below the main sensory relay, in the floor of the midline ventricle, with the hormone gland hanging from it on a stalk.

questions.text: Which of these is a main function of the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus controls homeostasis, including temperature, hunger and thirst.

questions.text: The hypothalamus controls which endocrine gland through a stalk?
questions.explanation: The pituitary hangs from the hypothalamus by the infundibulum and is controlled by it.

content.origin: Latin pituita, "phlegm" (it was once thought to make nasal mucus); hypophysis is Greek for "undergrowth".
content.location: At the base of the brain in the midline, sitting in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, just below the optic chiasm and hanging from the hypothalamus by the pituitary stalk.
content.description: A pea-sized gland with an anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and a posterior lobe (neurohypophysis).
content.function: The anterior lobe makes growth hormone, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH, controlling other endocrine glands. The posterior lobe releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus.
content.mnemonic: "Master gland under the master": the pituitary controls other glands but takes orders from the hypothalamus.
content.clinical: A pituitary tumour (adenoma) growing upwards can press on the optic chiasm, causing loss of the outer (temporal) half of vision in both eyes (bitemporal hemianopia).
content.hint: The pea-sized gland in the bony saddle of the skull base, hanging on a stalk just below where the optic nerves cross.

questions.text: A pituitary tumour pressing upwards typically causes which visual problem?
options: Double vision only when looking down
Loss of the lower half of vision
Loss of the outer half of vision in both eyes
questions.explanation: It compresses the crossing fibres in the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia.

questions.text: The pituitary gland sits in a hollow of which bone?
questions.explanation: It lies in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone.

content.origin: Latin pinea, "pine cone", from its shape.
content.location: In the midline at the back of the third ventricle, above the top of the midbrain (the superior colliculi) and below the splenium of the corpus callosum.
content.description: A tiny pine-cone-shaped gland attached to the back of the roof of the third ventricle. It often contains calcium deposits in adults.
content.function: Makes the hormone melatonin, mainly at night in darkness, helping to set the body's daily (circadian) sleep-wake rhythm.
content.mnemonic: "Pine cone at night": the pineal makes melatonin when the lights go out.
content.clinical: A pineal gland calcified with age is visible on CT scans and X-rays and serves as a midline landmark. Pineal tumours can block the cerebral aqueduct and cause hydrocephalus.
content.hint: A tiny cone-shaped gland at the back of the midline ventricle, perched above the top of the brainstem.

questions.text: Which hormone is produced by the pineal gland?
questions.explanation: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

content.origin: Greek hippos, "horse", and kampos, "sea monster": its curved shape looks like a seahorse.
content.location: In the medial part of the left temporal lobe, forming the floor of the inferior (temporal) horn of the lateral ventricle, just behind the amygdala.
content.description: A curved ridge of grey matter shaped like a seahorse. Its output fibres gather into the fornix. Only the left one is shown in this model; a matching one lies in the right hemisphere.
content.function: Part of the limbic system. It is essential for forming new long-term memories of facts and events, and for spatial memory and navigation.
content.mnemonic: "Hippo-campus goes to campus to learn": it is the brain's memory-maker.
content.clinical: The hippocampus is one of the first areas damaged in Alzheimer disease, which explains early loss of recent memory. It is also a common source of temporal lobe epilepsy.
content.hint: A seahorse-shaped ridge in the medial temporal lobe forming the floor of the temporal horn of the ventricle.

questions.text: What is the main function of the hippocampus?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is essential for forming new declarative (fact and event) memories.

questions.text: Which disease typically damages the hippocampus early, causing recent memory loss?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer disease affects the hippocampus early, impairing new memory formation.

content.origin: Greek amygdale, "almond", from its shape.
content.location: Deep in the front of the left medial temporal lobe, under the uncus, just in front of the hippocampus and the tip of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.
content.description: An almond-shaped cluster of nuclei. Only the left one is shown in this model; a matching one lies in the right hemisphere.
content.function: Part of the limbic system. It detects threats, generates fear and other emotional responses, and strengthens memories of emotional events.
content.mnemonic: "Amygdala = alarm": the almond-shaped alarm bell of the brain.
content.clinical: Damage to both amygdalae reduces normal fear responses and the ability to recognise fear in other people's faces.
content.hint: An almond-shaped cluster in the front of the medial temporal lobe, just in front of the seahorse-shaped memory structure.

questions.text: Which emotion is most closely linked with the amygdala?
questions.explanation: The amygdala detects threat and produces fear responses.

questions.text: The amygdala lies just in front of which structure?
questions.explanation: The amygdala sits in the anterior medial temporal lobe, in front of the hippocampus.

content.origin: Latin cauda, "tail": the nucleus has a long tail.
content.location: Deep in the left cerebral hemisphere, curving along the wall of the lateral ventricle; its head bulges into the anterior horn, lateral to the ventricle.
content.description: A C-shaped nucleus with a large head, a body and a thin tail that follows the lateral ventricle into the temporal lobe. It is one of the basal ganglia. Only the left one is shown in this model; a matching one lies in the right hemisphere.
content.function: With the putamen it forms the striatum, the input part of the basal ganglia. It helps start and control movement and is involved in learning, habits and motivation.
content.mnemonic: "Caudate has a tail": caudate plus putamen make the striped striatum.
content.clinical: In Huntington disease the caudate nucleus shrinks, which enlarges the anterior horns of the lateral ventricles on scans and causes involuntary jerky movements (chorea).
content.hint: A C-shaped grey-matter nucleus with a head and tail that hugs the wall of the lateral ventricle.

questions.text: Shrinkage of the caudate nucleus is characteristic of which disease?
questions.explanation: Huntington disease causes atrophy of the caudate nucleus.

questions.text: The caudate nucleus and putamen together form what?
questions.explanation: The caudate and putamen together are called the striatum.

content.origin: Latin putamen, "shell" or "husk" (of a nut): it forms the outer shell of the lentiform nucleus.
content.location: Deep in the left cerebral hemisphere, lateral to the globus pallidus and internal capsule and deep to the insula.
content.description: A rounded, shell-like mass that is the outer part of the lens-shaped lentiform nucleus. It is one of the basal ganglia. Only the left one is shown in this model; a matching one lies in the right hemisphere.
content.function: Part of the striatum (with the caudate). It receives input from the motor cortex and dopamine from the substantia nigra and helps regulate and smooth movement.
content.mnemonic: "Putamen = the outer shell": it wraps around the globus pallidus.
content.clinical: In Parkinson disease the dopamine supply to the putamen is lost first. The putamen is also a common site of bleeding in brain haemorrhage caused by high blood pressure.
content.hint: The outer shell of the lens-shaped deep nucleus, lying just beneath the hidden island of cortex.

questions.text: The putamen lies on which side of the globus pallidus?
questions.explanation: The putamen lies lateral to the globus pallidus; together they form the lentiform nucleus.

content.origin: Latin globus, "ball", and pallidus, "pale": it looks paler than the putamen because of its many myelinated fibres.
content.location: Deep in the left cerebral hemisphere, medial to the putamen and lateral to the internal capsule.
content.description: A pale, wedge-shaped mass with external and internal segments; with the putamen it forms the lentiform nucleus. It is one of the basal ganglia. Only the left one is shown in this model; a matching one lies in the right hemisphere.
content.function: The main output of the basal ganglia. Its internal segment sends inhibitory signals to the thalamus, helping to select wanted movements and suppress unwanted ones.
content.mnemonic: "Pale ball in the middle": the globus pallidus sits inside the putamen shell.
content.clinical: Deep brain stimulation of the internal globus pallidus is used to treat movement disorders such as Parkinson disease and dystonia.
content.hint: The pale, wedge-shaped inner part of the lens-shaped deep nucleus, medial to its outer shell.

questions.text: What is the main role of the globus pallidus?
options: Main output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus
questions.explanation: The internal globus pallidus sends the main inhibitory output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus.

content.origin: Latin fornix, "arch" or "vault".
content.location: Arching under the corpus callosum from the left hippocampus in the temporal lobe forward to above the third ventricle, then down to the mammillary body of the hypothalamus.
content.description: A C-shaped bundle of white-matter fibres. The two sides join under the corpus callosum (body of the fornix) and separate again at the front as the columns. Only the left one is shown in this model; a matching one lies in the right hemisphere.
content.function: The main output tract of the hippocampus, carrying memory-related signals to the mammillary bodies and other limbic areas, as part of the Papez circuit.
content.mnemonic: "Fornix = forward arch": it arches forward from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.
content.clinical: Damage to the fornix, for example during surgery for a colloid cyst of the third ventricle, can cause problems forming new memories.
content.hint: An arched white-matter tract that curves under the midline bridge between hemispheres, running from the seahorse-shaped memory structure towards the hypothalamus.

questions.text: The fornix carries output fibres from which structure?
questions.explanation: The fornix is the main efferent tract of the hippocampus.

content.origin: Greek chiasma, "a crossing", from the letter chi (X).
content.location: At the base of the brain in the midline, above the pituitary gland, in front of the pituitary stalk and just below the front of the hypothalamus.
content.description: An X-shaped structure where the two optic nerves meet and then separate into the two optic tracts.
content.function: Fibres from the nasal (inner) half of each retina cross here to the opposite side, so each side of the brain receives the opposite half of the visual field from both eyes.
content.mnemonic: "Chiasm = X marks the crossing": the nasal fibres cross.
content.clinical: Pressure from below, usually a pituitary tumour, damages the crossing fibres and causes bitemporal hemianopia (loss of both outer visual fields).
content.hint: An X-shaped crossing at the base of the brain, above the pea-sized gland, where the nerves from the eyes meet.

questions.text: Which fibres cross at the optic chiasm?
options: Fibres from the temporal (outer) half of each retina
Fibres from the nasal (inner) half of each retina
questions.explanation: Only the nasal retinal fibres cross, carrying the temporal visual fields.

content.origin: Latin ventriculus, "little belly"; lateralis, "at the side".
content.location: Inside the left cerebral hemisphere, below the corpus callosum, curving from the frontal lobe back and then down into the temporal lobe.
content.description: A C-shaped cavity with an anterior (frontal) horn, body, posterior (occipital) horn and inferior (temporal) horn. It contains choroid plexus, which produces cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
content.function: Holds and produces cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain, removes waste and helps keep pressure stable. CSF flows from here through the interventricular foramen into the third ventricle.
content.mnemonic: CSF route: "Lateral to third, through the aqueduct to the fourth, then out to the space around the brain".
content.clinical: If CSF flow is blocked, the ventricles swell (hydrocephalus), raising pressure in the skull. A shunt tube can drain the excess fluid.
content.hint: The largest C-shaped fluid-filled cavity inside each hemisphere, with horns reaching into the frontal, occipital and temporal lobes.

questions.text: Cerebrospinal fluid passes from each lateral ventricle into which space?
questions.explanation: CSF flows from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina into the third ventricle.

questions.text: Which tissue in the ventricles produces cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus in the ventricles secretes CSF.

content.origin: Latin ventriculus, "little belly"; lateralis, "at the side".
content.location: Inside the right cerebral hemisphere, below the corpus callosum, curving from the frontal lobe back and then down into the temporal lobe.
content.description: A C-shaped cavity with an anterior (frontal) horn, body, posterior (occipital) horn and inferior (temporal) horn. It contains choroid plexus, which produces cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
content.function: Holds and produces cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain, removes waste and helps keep pressure stable. CSF flows from here through the interventricular foramen into the third ventricle.
content.mnemonic: CSF route: "Lateral to third, through the aqueduct to the fourth, then out to the space around the brain".
content.clinical: If CSF flow is blocked, the ventricles swell (hydrocephalus), raising pressure in the skull. A shunt tube can drain the excess fluid.
content.hint: The largest C-shaped fluid-filled cavity inside each hemisphere, with horns reaching into the frontal, occipital and temporal lobes.

content.origin: Latin ventriculus tertius, "third little belly".
content.location: In the midline of the forebrain between the left and right thalami, with the hypothalamus in its floor and lower walls.
content.description: A narrow, slit-like cavity. It connects to each lateral ventricle through an interventricular foramen (of Monro) and to the fourth ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct.
content.function: Carries cerebrospinal fluid from the lateral ventricles to the cerebral aqueduct, and has its own choroid plexus in the roof that adds more CSF.
content.mnemonic: "Third is the thin one": a slit between the two thalami.
content.clinical: A colloid cyst in the front of the third ventricle can block the interventricular foramina, causing sudden hydrocephalus and headache.
content.hint: A thin slit of fluid in the midline, walled on each side by the egg-shaped relay masses.

questions.text: The third ventricle lies between which pair of structures?
questions.explanation: The third ventricle is a midline slit between the two thalami.

content.origin: Latin aqua, "water", and ducere, "to lead": a channel for fluid.
content.location: In the midline, running through the midbrain from the back of the third ventricle down to the fourth ventricle.
content.description: A narrow canal about 1.5 cm long, the narrowest part of the ventricular system. It has no choroid plexus.
content.function: Carries cerebrospinal fluid from the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle.
content.mnemonic: "Aqueduct = water pipe" through the midbrain.
content.clinical: Narrowing of the aqueduct (aqueductal stenosis) is a common cause of hydrocephalus present at birth, because CSF cannot drain from the third ventricle.
content.hint: The narrow fluid channel running through the upper brainstem between the slit-like midline cavity and the tent-shaped one behind the pons.

questions.text: The cerebral aqueduct connects which two ventricles?
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct runs through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle.

content.origin: Latin ventriculus quartus, "fourth little belly".
content.location: In the midline of the hindbrain, between the pons and upper medulla in front and the cerebellum behind.
content.description: A tent-shaped cavity with a diamond-shaped floor (the rhomboid fossa). It opens into the subarachnoid space through one median aperture and two lateral apertures, and continues down as the central canal of the spinal cord.
content.function: Receives CSF from the cerebral aqueduct, adds more from its choroid plexus, and releases it through its apertures into the subarachnoid space around the brain and spinal cord.
content.mnemonic: "Magendie in the middle, Luschka on the lateral sides": the three exits of the fourth ventricle.
content.clinical: Tumours of the cerebellum or brainstem in children can block the fourth ventricle, causing hydrocephalus with headache, vomiting and unsteadiness.
content.hint: A tent-shaped fluid cavity behind the pons and medulla, with the cerebellum forming its roof.

questions.text: The fourth ventricle lies between the brainstem and which structure?
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle is between the pons and medulla in front and the cerebellum behind.

questions.text: How does CSF leave the ventricular system?
options: Through the median and lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle
questions.explanation: CSF exits into the subarachnoid space through the apertures of the fourth ventricle.

content.origin: Greek mesos, "middle", and enkephalos, "brain".
content.location: The top part of the brainstem, between the diencephalon (thalamus and hypothalamus) above and the pons below, passing through the tentorial notch.
content.description: A short segment with the cerebral peduncles in front, the tectum (four bumps called colliculi) behind, and the cerebral aqueduct running through it. It contains the substantia nigra.
content.function: Carries motor and sensory tracts between the forebrain and lower brainstem. The superior colliculi help with visual reflexes and the inferior colliculi with hearing; it contains the nuclei of cranial nerves III and IV.
content.mnemonic: "Midbrain has 3 and 4": the oculomotor (III) and trochlear (IV) nerves start here.
content.clinical: In Parkinson disease, dopamine-making neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain die, causing tremor, stiffness and slow movement.
content.hint: The top segment of the brainstem, with four small bumps on its back and a narrow fluid channel through its centre.

questions.text: Parkinson disease involves loss of neurons in which part of the brain?
questions.explanation: Dopamine-producing neurons of the substantia nigra, in the midbrain, are lost in Parkinson disease.

questions.text: Which cranial nerves arise from the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor (III) and trochlear (IV) nerves arise from the midbrain.

content.origin: Latin pons, "bridge": it looks like a bridge between the two halves of the cerebellum.
content.location: The middle part of the brainstem, between the midbrain above and the medulla oblongata below, in front of the cerebellum and fourth ventricle.
content.description: A rounded bulge on the front of the brainstem made of transverse fibres, joined to the cerebellum on each side by the middle cerebellar peduncles.
content.function: Relays signals from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum, helps regulate breathing rhythm, and contains nuclei of cranial nerves V to VIII (trigeminal, abducens, facial and vestibulocochlear).
content.mnemonic: "Pons = bridge": it bridges the cortex to the cerebellum.
content.clinical: A stroke in the front of the pons (usually from basilar artery blockage) can cause locked-in syndrome: the person is awake and aware but can move only the eyes up and down.
content.hint: The rounded bulge in the middle of the brainstem, between the upper segment and the lowest part joining the spinal cord.

questions.text: Which part of the brainstem lies between the midbrain and the medulla oblongata?
questions.explanation: The pons is the middle part of the brainstem.

questions.text: Locked-in syndrome most often results from damage to which structure?
questions.explanation: A stroke in the ventral pons interrupts motor tracts but spares consciousness.

content.origin: Latin medulla, "marrow" or "core", and oblongata, "elongated".
content.location: The lowest part of the brainstem, below the pons and in front of the cerebellum, continuing into the spinal cord at the foramen magnum.
content.description: A cone-shaped segment with two pyramids on its front surface and an olive on each side. The motor fibres of the pyramids cross here (decussation of the pyramids).
content.function: Contains vital centres controlling heart rate, blood pressure and breathing, and reflexes such as swallowing, coughing and vomiting. It holds nuclei of cranial nerves IX to XII.
content.mnemonic: "Medulla = most vital": damage here stops breathing and heartbeat control.
content.clinical: Raised pressure in the skull can force the cerebellar tonsils down through the foramen magnum (tonsillar herniation), compressing the medulla and causing breathing to stop.
content.hint: The lowest part of the brainstem, tapering into the spinal cord at the big hole in the skull base.

questions.text: Which vital function is controlled by the medulla oblongata?
questions.explanation: The medulla contains the cardiovascular and respiratory centres.

questions.text: Where do the motor (pyramidal) fibres cross to the opposite side?
questions.explanation: The decussation of the pyramids is in the lower medulla.

content.origin: Latin cerebellum, "little brain".
content.location: At the back of the skull in the posterior cranial fossa, below the occipital lobes (separated by the tentorium cerebelli) and behind the pons and medulla.
content.description: Two hemispheres joined by a narrow midline vermis, with a surface of fine parallel folds (folia). Inside, its white matter branches like a tree (arbor vitae). Three pairs of peduncles connect it to the brainstem.
content.function: Coordinates movement, balance, posture and muscle tone, and helps learn motor skills. Each side controls the same side of the body.
content.mnemonic: "Cerebellum = balance-ellum": the little brain that keeps you steady.
content.clinical: Cerebellar damage, including from alcohol, causes ataxia: an unsteady wide-based walk, poor coordination, intention tremor and slurred speech, on the same side as the lesion.
content.hint: The "little brain" with fine parallel folds, tucked under the back of the hemispheres behind the brainstem.

questions.text: What is the main function of the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture.

questions.text: Damage to the right cerebellar hemisphere causes poor coordination on which side?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum controls the same (ipsilateral) side of the body.
